seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Ulysses published thanks for all your help.

div.note: This telegram was handed in at “12 h” (noon) on 2 February 1922 and is addressed to “M Ezra Pound, rue Notre Dame des Champs, 70 bis.” Tired of London, which he had come to feel was morally and culturally enervated, Pound left that city in late 1920 and, after staying for several months at the Hotel du Pas de Calais in Paris, took a three-year lease for himself and his wife Dorothy on a spacious studio off rue Notre Dame des Champs around the beginning of December 1921. He wrote his father that he had “built two armchairs kitch tabl. chinese dining table. – also wash stand, & stool plus shelves, screws etc.” (Ezra Pound to His Parents: Letters 1895-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 490). Pound made a sketch of the new accommodations for his parents (ibid., 491); photographs of the studio have survived, including a famous one of Pound, John Quinn, Ford Madox Ford, and JJ. Ford and JJ are sitting in chairs constructed by Pound (see Ellmann, JJ photo insert XXXVI).

note.p: JJ’s masterwork Ulysses was first published as a complete book on his fortieth birthday, 2 February 1922, through Sylvia Beach’s Paris bookshop, Shakespeare and Company. The book’s Dijon printer, Maurice Darantiere, dispatched two copies by an express train, which Beach met early on the morning of 2 February. “In less than ten minutes her taxi brought her to Joyce’s door; she turned over one copy to him and kept the other to exhibit in her shop” (Ellmann, JJ 524). The edition was privately subscribed and limited to 1,000 copies, of which 100, signed by JJ, were printed on Dutch handmade paper and sold for 350 francs each; 150 copies were on vergé d’Arches for 250 francs each; and 750 copies were on handmade paper for 150 francs each. The large, bulky volume was bound in blue paper covers with “ULYSSES | BY | JAMES JOYCE” on the front in white lettering – the effect evocative of the colors of the Greek flag. The book ran to 732 pages, not counting front and back matter.

Ulysses was printed for Shakespeare and Company eleven times over the years (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 24-27). The complicated story of the sales of the first edition to private subscribers, collectors, and booksellers, along with JJ’s large share of the net profits, is told in “Consuming Investments: Joyce’s Ulysses,” chapter 2 of Lawrence Rainey’s Institutions of Modernism: Literary Elites and Public Culture (New Haven, CT: Yale University Press, 1998), 42-76. The first English edition appeared under the imprint of the Egoist Press, assisted by John Rodker in Paris, on 12 October 1922.
